MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents

A benchmark that scores LLM-based multi-agent systems on both task success and coordination quality, across four cooperative scenarios (Research, Minecraft, Database, Coding) and two competitive ones (Werewolf, Bargaining), while treating coordination topology and planning strategy as first-class experimental variables rather than implementation details.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By the time MultiAgentBench was posted in March 2025, LLM-based multi-agent systems were already common in practice — MetaGPT and AutoGen coordinating software-development teams, CAMEL and AgentVerse exploring "society of agents" dynamics, Generative Agents simulating whole neighborhoods of interacting personas — but the benchmarks used to evaluate any of this were still single-agent instruments. The paper is explicit about the target: prior agent benchmarks "such as AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023), VisualAgentBench (Sun et al., 2023), GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), ToolBench (Qin et al., 2024) and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) primarily focus on isolated reasoning and generation, overlooking the dynamics intrinsic to multi-agent interactions." Two gaps stand out. First, domain narrowness: existing multi-agent work each targets one setting — coding, or Minecraft, or a social-deduction game — rather than a shared instrument spanning several. Second, and more structural: no existing benchmark cleanly separates whether a team's coordination process was any good from whether the team's final output was any good. A team can stumble into a correct answer through terrible communication, or communicate fluently and still fail the task, and a single task-success number conflates the two. MultiAgentBench targets both gaps at once: six scenarios split evenly between "mutual goal" task-oriented settings and "conflicting goal" competitive settings, run through a framework (MARBLE) that varies the coordination topology and planning strategy as explicit experimental axes.

// how it works

The method

MultiAgentBench's evaluation harness, MARBLE (Multi-agent cooRdination Backbone with LLM Engine), centers on a Coordination Engine that ingests a Configuration — task info, agent persona data, and a domain database — and builds an Agent Graph G = (A, E): a set of agents A and typed relationship edges (aᵢ, r, aⱼ), where r is, for example, collaborates, supervises, or negotiates. Which agents are even allowed to talk to each other is therefore an explicit, inspectable graph rather than an implicit prompting convention. Each agent's Cognitive Module tracks persona, inter-agent relationships, and reasoning strategy, and draws on a Shared Memory split into per-agent long-term memory (retrieved via RAG) and short-term memory; a Communication Module handles message exchange, and an Action Module executes decisions via function calling against the scenario's Environment and Tool Box. Every run terminates at an Evaluator that reports both a Task Score and a Coordination (Collaboration) Score.

Two design axes are varied independently rather than fixed by convention. The first is coordination protocol: centralized Star (a single planner assigns tasks to actors and consolidates their feedback) and Tree (a top-level planner delegates to sub-planners, which manage actors below them), versus decentralized Graph-Mesh (a fully interconnected network of actors that plan concurrently) and Chain (actors hand decisions sequentially down a line). The second is planning-prompt strategy, applied to the centralized planner role: Vanilla zero-shot instruction; Chain-of-Thought, which feeds the planner the target task, agent profiles, and prior-subtask summaries; Group Discussion, where agents share constraints and jointly refine the plan; and Cognitive (Self-)Evolving Planning, modeled on Reflexion, which has the planner generate an expected outcome per task, store it in memory, and compare it against the actual result on the next iteration to accumulate "evolving experience."

The benchmark spans four mutual-goal, task-oriented scenarios and two conflicting-goal, social-simulation scenarios. On the mutual-goal side: Research has agents with complementary profiles — drawn from 100 curated ML/AI papers via the ResearchTown dataset, split into 33 easy, 34 medium, and 33 hard tasks — co-author a proposal in a fixed five-question format (what's the problem, why it matters, why it's hard, why it hasn't been solved, and what the approach is), using tools like get_related_papers and get_paper_by_arxiv_id. Minecraft has agents jointly construct a target structure, scored by a block-level hit rate. Database drops agents into a PostgreSQL instance (run in Docker) seeded with one of five anomaly types — Fetch/Insert Large Data, Lock Contention, Redundant Index, or Vacuum — and has them diagnose up to two predicted root causes by querying system views such as pg_locks and pg_stat_statements. Coding, adapted from the SRDD dataset, has agents with complementary specialties (debugging, execution, test-writing, review) build software across five topic areas (Education, Work, Life, Game, Creation). On the conflicting-goal side: Werewolf is the social-deduction game, run both as single-day partial simulations loaded from one of 100 saved game archives and as full-game simulations, with agents split into adversarial factions (villagers vs. werewolves, plus special roles like Seer and Witch). Bargaining simulates multi-party negotiation over a shared item — one example task is negotiating a "Chair Banner" listed at "$14.99 with a rating of 4.8/5 stars" — where buyer and seller each try to maximize individual gain.

Every scenario reports two families of scores. Task Completion has two parts: a milestone-based KPI, where an LLM continuously monitors the interaction log for whether task-specific milestones (e.g., completing or improving a five-question research proposal) have been reached, crediting every contributing agent; and a separate task-based score — an LLM rubric for Research and Bargaining, a rule-based metric (accuracy or hit rate) for Minecraft, Werewolf, Database, and Coding. Coordination is a Communication Score and a Planning Score, each an LLM-judged 0–5 rating (0 if no communication occurs at all) over the task description, agent profiles, and the aggregated communication/planning transcript; the two are averaged into an overall Coordination Score.

KPIoverall = 1N Σj=1..N KPIj  =  1NM Σj=1..N nj // n_j = milestones agent j contributed to; M = total milestones; N = number of agents
// what they found

The results

The main experiment runs five models — three open-weight (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B, Meta-Llama-3.1-70B, Meta-Llama-3.3-70B, served via TogetherAI) and two closed (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, gpt-4o-mini) — through all six scenarios under the Graph-Mesh protocol, the paper's default. Averaging each model's six per-scenario Task Scores from Table 1 by hand: gpt-4o-mini comes out on top at ≈52.7% (84.13 Research, 33.60 Minecraft, 45.00 Database, 65.10 Coding, 74.47 Bargaining, 14.06 WereWolf), ahead of Meta-Llama-3.1-70B at ≈48.0% — consistent with the paper's claim that "gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score." Coordination Score, though, tells a more scenario-specific story: in Minecraft, Meta-Llama-3.1-70B posts a Coordination Score of 75.00 — the highest value in that column — while its own Task Score is 0.21%, the worst in the entire table. The paper reads this as evidence that "coordination... does not compensate for inherent deficiencies in task execution," and an appendix analysis traces the actual mechanism: Meta-Llama-3.1-70B's Minecraft function calls are executable less than half the time, versus close to 100% for both GPT models and around 80% for the other two Llama models — so this particular gap is a tool-use/format-following failure specific to one model and scenario, not evidence of a general coordination/execution trade-off.

A second experiment isolates the coordination-protocol and planning-strategy axes — but only in the Research scenario. Across Star, Tree, Graph, and Chain, the paper reports that "the graph-based protocol excels in research scenarios with the best task performance, planning efficiency, and token usage, while both the star and graph protocols yield similar task scores," whereas "the tree-based protocol performs poorly, with high token consumption and the lowest task and coordination scores." Across the four planning strategies, Cognitive Evolving Planning posts the highest Coordination Score (59.00, vs. 55.50 Naive, 50.00 CoT, 49.00 Group) and a Task Score (76.67) close to the best, Chain-of-Thought's 77.67; Group Discussion is lowest on every metric shown — KPI (46.35), Coordination Score (49.00), and Task Score (72.67) — which the authors attribute to an "overly large planning group" hindering effectiveness, "similar to large organizations in real-world scenarios."

The Werewolf scenario supplies the paper's most concrete "emergent behavior" evidence: Meta-Llama-3.3-70B reaches a villager win rate of "around 35%," clearly ahead of Meta-Llama-3.1-8B's 1.15% and gpt-4o-mini's 3.09%, and even outperforms the gpt-4o agents that generated the underlying 100 saved-game archives — a positive net score of 0.4511 versus gpt-4o's −2.1946, and a 35% villager win rate versus gpt-4o's own 24.73%. Case studies trace this to specific behaviors: a Llama-3.1-8B Seer that "repeatedly emphasizes its innocence... yet fails to provide concrete inspection results," and a gpt-4o Seer/Witch pair that is "overly cautious, missing optimal sharing opportunities" and losing as a result.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

MultiAgentBench is a genuine step up in breadth — six scenarios, four topologies, four planning strategies scored on both task success and coordination in one paper — but several of its own headline claims don't survive being checked against its own tables and appendix, and the LLM-as-judge machinery underneath every Coordination Score is validated in exactly one of six scenarios.

Start with Table 1's own caption: it claims "CS is a good indicator for TS given three pairs of scenarios having the one model having the highest TS and CS at the same time." Checking all six scenario columns against each other, only two actually show this — Bargaining (gpt-4o-mini tops both TS at 74.47 and CS at 74.20) and WereWolf (Meta-Llama-3.3-70B tops both TS at 36.33 and CS at 76.30). In Research, Minecraft, Database, and Coding, the model with the highest TS and the model with the highest CS are different models. The abstract makes a second checkable claim — "cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%" — but Figure 6's own KPI numbers show Cognitive Evolve Planning at 49.87%, lower than Naive's 52.37%, not 3 points higher; whatever the "3%" figure refers to, it is not the KPI column plotted in Figure 6.

The human-validation appendix (Table 2, Werewolf scenario only) is meant to license every LLM-judged Communication/Planning score in the paper, but its own text understates its own biggest gap: it states "the largest difference in communication scores among these models is within 0.38 (e.g., gpt3.5-turbo achieves 3.75 in human evaluation vs. 4.00 in machine evaluation)" — a 0.25-point gap, not 0.38 (0.38 is actually llama31_8b's own human/machine gap, 2.62 vs. 3.00) — while the table's actual largest communication-score gap is gpt-4o-mini's 3.61 (human) vs. 3.00 (machine), a 0.61-point discrepancy, roughly 1.6× the 0.38 bound the text asserts and specifically on the model the paper spotlights as its Task Score leader.

baselines

Five models — three Llama (8B/70B/70B) and two OpenAI (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o-mini) — chosen because MARBLE "required function-calling abilities." No GPT-4, Claude, or any reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, cited in the intro) appears in this five-model roster scored across the six main scenarios; gpt-4o itself shows up only once, as the archive-generating baseline re-scored in the Werewolf full-run appendix table, not as a peer in the main comparison. So "model capabilities are the decisive factor" rests on a narrow, function-calling-filtered slice of the field.

contamination

Not classic train/test leakage, but a structural confound: the 100 Werewolf archives every model is scored against were "all played by GPT-4o-based agents" — so every model's Werewolf coordination is measured against a story world authored in GPT-4o's own conversational idiom, which could advantage or disadvantage models by stylistic proximity rather than genuine multi-agent skill.

what's missed

The coordination-protocol ablation (Star/Tree/Graph/Chain, Figure 5) and the planning-strategy ablation (Figure 6) are both run only in the Research scenario, yet Graph-Mesh is then adopted as the fixed default protocol for all six scenarios in the main experiment — so we never learn whether the protocol ranking that justified that default choice actually holds in Minecraft, Database, Coding, Bargaining, or Werewolf.

would raise confidence

Extending the human-alignment check beyond Werewolf Communication/Planning to the Research/Bargaining rubric scores and to the KPI milestone detector itself; re-running the protocol and planning ablations in at least one competitive scenario; and a corrected Appendix A.3 that reports its own largest human-vs-machine gap accurately.

// bottom line

Treat MultiAgentBench's protocol and planning-strategy rankings (Graph-Mesh best overall, Cognitive Evolve Planning best on Coordination Score only, Group Discussion worst on every metric shown) as a Research-scenario-specific finding, not an established law of multi-agent coordination — and treat the paper's own summary claims about Table 1 and Figure 6 as worth re-deriving from the raw cells before citing them.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. MultiAgentBench, via the MARBLE engine, is a benchmark that scores LLM-based multi-agent systems on both mutual-goal task-oriented scenarios (Research, Minecraft, Database, Coding) and conflicting-goal social-simulation scenarios (Werewolf, Bargaining) — pairing every result with a Task Score and a milestone/communication/planning-based Coordination Score, rather than task success alone.
  2. Across five models and six scenarios, gpt-4o-mini posts the highest averaged Task Score, but Coordination Score is a genuinely separate axis: Meta-Llama-3.1-70B pairs a 75.00 Minecraft Coordination Score with a 0.21% Task Score, because barely half its function calls in that scenario execute — a high Coordination Score does not rescue broken tool use.
  3. On coordination protocols and planning strategies — tested in the Research scenario only — Graph-Mesh topology comes out ahead of Star/Tree/Chain, and Cognitive Evolving Planning leads only on Coordination Score (59.00 vs. Naive's 55.50), trailing Naive on KPI (49.87 vs. 52.37) and COT on Task Score (76.67 vs. 77.67); read these as a starting hypothesis, since neither ablation is repeated in any of the other five scenarios before Graph-Mesh becomes the paper's fixed default.
